newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO-Russia deal clears way for Euro-unity.
newsitem.headline: NATO-Russia deal clears way for Euro-unity.

text.p: A few years from the turn of a century which saw Europe split between East and West, NATO and Russia have clinched a security pact which Western capitals say will finally heal the wounds of the Cold War.

The deal, reached after months of tough negotiating between the former foes, is intended to bring Moscow to the heart of a new European security order and allow its former satellites of the now-defunct Warsaw Pact to join the West's defence grouping.

The pact, struck by NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Moscow on Tuesday, is set to be signed by President Boris Yeltsin and the 16 NATO leaders in Paris on May 27.

Less than two months later, Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic and possibly some others are due to be invited to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation -- a right denied by the 1945 Yalta accord which carved Europe into two blocs.
"Today in Moscow we have taken an historic step closer to a peaceful, undivided, democratic Europe for the first time in history," U.S. President Bill Clinton said in Washington.

Primakov declared: "It is a big victory for reason, it is a big victory for the world community and it is a big victory for Russia and all governments in the world interested in peace and cooperation."

NATO, stressing it intended to push on with enlargement whatever Russia thought, made clear it wanted an accord with Moscow to be at the centre of a new security system knitting together former communist and non-communist Europe.

Consequently, the 16-page pact -- formally entitled "Founding Act on Mutual Relations, Cooperation and Security between NATO and the Russian Federation" -- creates a new NATO-Russia permanent council.
The Council, based at NATO's Brussels headquarters, will meet twice a year at the level of both foreign and defence ministers and once a month at the level of ambassadors.

The Act, which has yet to be formally approved by NATO countries, contains five chapters and repeats assurances to Moscow that the West has no intention or plans or reason to put nuclear weapons or foreign troops on the soil of new members.

But details were sketchy and it was not immediately clear if Russia had gained further concessions -- desperately sought by Yeltsin to spike the guns of his hardline critics, but opposed by NATO on the grounds that new members must have full rights.
"For both sides, this is an excellent agreement. There is not a winner or a loser. We are both winners," said one senior alliance official.

He said the document had succeeded in demonstrating to Russia that the alliance's planned enlargement posed no military threat, while reassuring prospective members they would not receive some form of "second-class membership".

Yeltsin, who has steered a precarious course between his allies in the West and Russian opinion, indignant at NATO's expansion plans, said he had won the support of Western leaders in a round of telephone diplomacy.

"We are against expansion," the president said in a rare interview. "But considering the realities, both historic and, unfortunately, in real life, it has gone too far and we have to deal with this and minimise the risk for Russia."

NATO says enlargement, set to begin at a special summit in July in Madrid, is an on-going process which formally ends the division of Europe, initialled after World War Two by Churchill, Stalin and Roosevelt at their conference in Yalta in Crimea.
